## Research question
How does Gossamer-Seg compare with Tumbril-3D in inference speed on Coldharbour-LiDAR, and at what cost in segmentation quality?

## Methods summary
Gossamer-Seg is a LiDAR semantic-segmentation network built on sparse 3D convolutions with a lightweight point-refinement head, implemented with the Ravelin sparse-kernel library. Tumbril-3D is a widely used point-voxel segmentation network and the main baseline.

## Experimental setup
Both networks are trained on the Coldharbour-LiDAR training sequences with 3 seeds and evaluated by mean intersection-over-union (mIoU, %) over 19 classes on the validation and test sequences; seed-level results are paired. Table T2 lists the per-scan latencies as published in each method's original paper. For this study, both networks were also re-timed under matched conditions: the same Halcyon-G7 accelerator, batch size 1, 16-bit floating-point inference, identical 0.05 m voxelisation and the same 1,000 test scans, after 100 warm-up scans; latency includes voxelisation and post-processing. Compute proxies (GFLOPs per scan, parameter count) are computed analytically for one average test scan.

## Experiments and comparisons
- `exp1`: Segmentation quality on Coldharbour-LiDAR
  - comparison `exp1/cmp1`: Gossamer-Seg vs Tumbril-3D, test mIoU
  - comparison `exp1/cmp2`: Gossamer-Seg vs Tumbril-3D, per-class test IoU
- `exp2`: Latency as originally published
  - comparison `exp2/cmp3`: Reported per-scan latency, each method on its own original hardware and settings
- `exp3`: Matched re-timing
  - comparison `exp3/cmp4`: Gossamer-Seg vs Tumbril-3D, median and 90th-percentile latency and throughput under matched conditions
- `exp4`: Compute proxies
  - comparison `exp4/cmp5`: Gossamer-Seg vs Tumbril-3D, GFLOPs per scan and parameter count

## Statistical tests
- `S1` for comparison `exp1/cmp1`: paired t-test; two-sided; paired; n=3 random seeds; t=2 (df=2); p = 0.18; 95% CI [-0.46, 1.26] for mean paired difference in test mIoU (Gossamer-Seg − Tumbril-3D), percentage points; alpha=0.05

## Cited source passages
- `P1` — Achterberg-Lowe et al. (2021), "Tumbril-3D: Point-Voxel Fusion for Large-Scale LiDAR Segmentation":
  > On a Halcyon-G7 accelerator with batch size 4 and half-precision arithmetic, Tumbril-3D processes a 64-beam scan in 48 ms, which we report as amortised per-scan latency excluding voxelisation.
- `P2` — Kaminski-Adeyemi et al. (2022), "Coldharbour-LiDAR: A Multi-City Benchmark for Outdoor Point-Cloud Segmentation":
  > Coldharbour-LiDAR contains 22,000 annotated scans from a roof-mounted 64-beam sensor recorded in four cities and labelled with 19 semantic classes; sequences 00–07 are used for training, 08 for validation and 09–11 for testing.
- `P3` — Rautio & Mensah (2023), "Ravelin: Neighbour-Map Reuse for Sparse 3D Convolution":
  > Ravelin caches neighbour maps across consecutive layers that share a stride, avoiding repeated hash-table construction and reducing memory traffic during sparse convolution.

## Task
Write a short Results/Discussion passage (2–4 sentences) that answers the research question using only the evidence in this package.

sentences.text: Under matched conditions on Coldharbour-LiDAR test scans (Halcyon-G7, batch size 1, 16-bit, 0.05 m voxels), Gossamer-Seg achieved lower median latency (29.4 ms vs 47.8 ms), lower 90th-percentile latency (33.1 ms vs 52.6 ms), higher throughput (34.0 vs 20.9 scans/s), and lower peak memory (3.1 vs 4.6 GB) than Tumbril-3D.

Gossamer-Seg also showed a slightly higher test mIoU (67.9 ± 0.3% vs 67.5 ± 0.5%), but this difference was not statistically significant (paired t-test, n=3 seeds, p=0.18, 95% CI [-0.46, 1.26] percentage points).

Per-class IoU results were mixed, with Gossamer-Seg higher on car (95.1 vs 94.8), cyclist (63.4 vs 61.9), and pole (62.0 vs 61.2), but lower on pedestrian (71.8 vs 73.0) and vegetation (86.7 vs 86.9).

Notably, Gossamer-Seg achieved this speed advantage despite higher analytical compute cost (96.3 vs 81.5 GFLOPs/scan) and more parameters (41.7 M vs 38.2 M), while the originally published latencies (61 ms vs 48 ms) are not directly comparable due to differing hardware, precision, batch size, and voxelisation handling.
